Learning Objectives
Identify the histologic features of tumors used to assess tumor grade.
Compare the relationship between tumor grade and tumor stage.
Review the role of tumor grade with regard to patient prognosis and treatment.
Introduction

Introduction
Tumors are graded according to their histologic appearance on microscopic
examination. Tumor grading represents biologic aggressiveness and predicts the risk for
distant metastatic spread. Grade often is assigned on biopsy to drive management

Grading Criteria
The French Federation of Cancer Centers Sarcoma Group (FNCLCC) is the most common
system used for grading sarcomas1-4 (Resource 1).
Grading includes the following histologic features:1-4:
Histologic subtype
Tumor differentiation
Mitotic activity
Necrosis
Cellularity, cytologic atypia/pleomorphism
FNCLCC grades (Figure 1)
Grade 1: well-differentiated, low grade
Grade 2: moderately differentiated, intermediate grade
Grade 3: poorly differentiated, high grade
Dedifferentiated

Figure 1
Histopathologic findings in chondrosarcoma are shown by advancing grade. Grade 1
chondrosarcoma/low-grade cartilage neoplasm (A) histologically appears similar to
enchondroma, with bland, hyaline cartilage. Features distinguishing low-grade from benign
lesions include disorganization, hypercellularity, increased nuclear detail, and more-than-
occasional binuclear cells. Grade 2 chondrosarcoma (B) demonstrates more malignant features,
with most cells having nuclear membranes and nucleoli becoming more prominent. The overall
architecture (C) remains lobular, but myxoid matrix replaces the lacunar architecture
characteristic of hyaline cartilage. Grade 3 chondrosarcoma (D) has all the cytologic features of
high-grade sarcoma, including pleomorphism, anaplasia, open chromatin, and frequent mitoses.
Differentiated chondrosarcoma (E) has features of low-grade chondrosarcoma (left) directly
apposed to a high-grade sarcoma. (Reproduced from McGough RL III: Chondrosarcoma of bone,
in Biermann JS, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 181-193.)

FNCLCC grades
Two main systems historically have been used for grading sarcoma. These include the
FNCLCC and National Cancers Institute systems for soft-tissue sarcoma1-4 (Resource 1).
Pathology reports are required to specify the grading system used. The World Health

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004040

Organization classification system and the College of American Pathologists Protocols
primarily follow the FNCLCC system.
The FNCLCC system evaluates each of the following histologic features using a three-
point scale: histologic subtype, tumor differentiation (extent to which the tissue
morphologically resembles normal tissue), mitotic count (amount of mitosis per 10 high-
power fields of view), percentage of necrosis (percentage of necrotic tissue throughout
the total examined tumor tissue), cellularity and cytologic atypia/pleoporphism.1-4 An
overall score is calculated, which corresponds with the assigned grade.3 Grade 1 (low-
grade) tumors are well differentiated, meaning that they highly resemble the tissue of
origin. Grade 2 (intermediate-grade) tumors are considered moderately differentiated,
whereas grade 3 (high-grade) tumors are poorly differentiated. Dedifferentiation refers
to a high-grade tumor that has completely lost the morphology or cellular/molecular
markers indicative of the primary tumor or tissue/cell of origin. Dedifferentiated tumors
often arise abruptly within a low-grade/well-differentiated tumor. Prognosis depends on
the specific tumor type but often portends poorer outcomes than conventional grade 3
tumors. Therefore, in some circumstances, these tumors may be referred to as grade 4
(ie, dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma); however, use of the term grade 4 remains a
subject of debate and varies between institutions.
Special Considerations
Tumor grade is particularly subject to sampling bias if a limited biopsy is obtained.
Chordomas typically are not graded. They are considered low grade but locally aggressive and
tend to metastasize later in their clinical course.1
Diagnosis and grading of low-grade cartilage lesions is inherently difficult, and biopsy of
lesions suspected to be enchondroma is not recommended.1
Grading may be deferred for specific histologic subtypes considered to be inherently low- or
high-grade by nature.2

Special Considerations

Tumor grade is particularly subject to sampling bias if a limited biopsy is obtained. MRI
of bone and soft-tissues lesions is recommended before biopsy for many reasons;
however, MRI may be particularly helpful in guiding the location for biopsy, especially if
considerable heterogeneity or features suggestive of dedifferentiation exist. Surgeons
should biopsy the area of the lesion that appears the highest grade or dedifferentiated.
Grading of conventional chondrosarcoma is primarily based on cellularity, cytologic
atypia, and mitotic figures and, therefore, is inherently difficult given the subtle histologic
differences between grades, the subjective nature of grading, and sampling error with
limited biopsy specimens. Distinguishing enchondroma from grade 1 chondrosarcoma is
a particular diagnostic challenge because the two pathologies may appear identical
under a microscope; therefore, biopsy of suspected enchondroma is not
recommended.1
Certain sarcoma subtypes typically are not graded. Chordomas typically are considered
low grade but are locally aggressive. They can metastasize but often do so later in their
clinical course.1 Grading of the following soft-tissue sarcomas generally is not
recommended because they characteristically behave aggressively and are considered
inherently high grade: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, embryonal and alveolar
rhabdomyosarcoma, angiosarcoma, extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma, alveolar
soft-part sarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, and epithelioid sarcoma.2
Grade Versus Stage
Tumor grade represents the biologic aggressiveness of the tumor and its propensity to
metastasize. Although it is an important variable in tumor staging systems, it does not factor in
a patient’s current/overall disease burden, dissimilar from tumor stage.

Grade Versus Stage
The grade is a level of aggressiveness assigned to a tumor based on histologic
evaluation. The grade is an attempt to understand the biologic aggressiveness of the

9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Grading of Tumors
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004040
5/9

tumor cells and the risk of metastatic potential. The stage is assigned to the patient and
is an assessment of the overall tumor burden and extent of disease at that moment in
time. The tumor grade is one part of the assessment for staging. Some staging systems
use a two-tier scale (low versus high) rather than a three-point scale (G1, G2, G3). For the
latter, G1 is considered low grade, and G2, G3, and dedifferentiated are considered high
grade.2
Prognostic Importance
Tumor grade is the most important predictor of metastatic risk and is a major overall
prognostic factor, second only to metastasis (including discontinuous tumor/skip metastasis in
bone sarcoma).
Although the metastatic potential of sarcoma is specific to the subtype, the metastatic risk of
low-, intermediate-, and high-grade tumors generally is less than 10%, 10% to 30%, and greater
than 30% respectively5 (Resource 2).
Treatment Implications
Low-grade tumors typically are not managed via neoadjuvant therapies, such as radiation
therapy or chemotherapy.

Treatment Implications
Low-grade tumors are associated with low rates of local recurrence and distant
metastasis. Although some exceptions may exist, they typically are not managed via
neoadjuvant therapies, such as radiation therapy or chemotherapy because the
advantages in these cases often do not outweigh the risks.
